app_claim: Tre’r Ceiri phase 2: “Abandoned hillfort” from 400 onward, size 0.
problem: The phase label states that the hillfort was abandoned after AD 400, but Coflein says occupation was ‘sporadic’ and likely extended into the early medieval period. The app’s uncertainty note only acknowledges use ‘until at least the 4th century’, so it omits that continuation.

evidence.title: Tre’r Ceiri hillfort (NPRN 95292), site record
evidence.publisher: Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (Coflein)
evidence.what_it_says: Coflein describes it as a long-lived Iron Age and Roman hillfort ‘with sporadic occupation likely to have extended into the early medieval period’ and says excavation shows use until at least the 4th century AD.

$[3].phases[2].label: No certain hillfort occupation; sporadic use may have continued into the early medieval period
$[3].phases[2].note: Coflein says sporadic occupation likely extended into the early medieval period; AD 400 is only the end of the well-attested Roman-period use.

new_values.$[3].uncertainty: Coflein gives only ‘later Iron Age’ for the foundation and says occupation was sporadic and likely extended into the early medieval period; the years 200 BC and AD 400 are placeholders for those phrases. A Bronze Age cairn on the summit is older than the fort.

app_claim: Parys Mountain phase 0: “Bronze Age copper workings” from -1900 to -1500; phase 2: “Possible Roman copper working” from 78 to 400, size 1. Summary: “Roman working is inferred from stamped copper ingots found on Anglesey and Pleiades lists it as a Roman mine.”
problem: The app’s Bronze Age span is broader and differently centred from the only available Bayesian model. The 2021 Parys Mountain study models the first mining in 2245–1785 cal BC (95%; probably 2085–1890) and the end in 1815–1300 cal BC (95%; probably 1735–1485). More importantly, the same study says that despite efforts to identify and date Roman underground workings, none has yet been identified and the current chronology does not extend beyond the Early Bronze Age. A visible size-1 Roman phase is therefore more definite than the evidence, even though the uncertainty note calls it an inference.

evidence.title: The Bronze Age Copper Mines of Parys Mountain, north Wales: Survey, Excavation and Bayesian Modelling
evidence.publisher: Cambridge University Press on behalf of the Prehistoric Society
evidence.what_it_says: The model estimates that mining activity first took place in 2245–1785 cal BC (95% probability), probably 2085–1890 cal BC, and finished in 1815–1300 cal BC, probably 1735–1485 cal BC. It also states that no Roman underground workings have yet been identified and the current chronology does not extend beyond the Early Bronze Age.

evidence.title: Parys Mountain (Pleiades place 82297)
evidence.what_it_says: The Pleiades record is only a brief gazetteer entry: “Roman mine on Parys Mountain, Wales,” with no date or excavation evidence.

$[5].phases[0].label: Early Bronze Age copper workings
$[5].phases[0].note: Bayesian model: start 2245–1785 cal BC (95%), probably 2085–1890; end 1815–1300 cal BC (95%), probably 1735–1485.

$[5].phases[2].label: No dated Roman workings
$[5].phases[2].note: Pleiades calls Parys Mountain a Roman mine, but the 2021 study found no dated Roman underground workings and says the chronology does not extend beyond the Early Bronze Age.

new_values.$[5].summary: A copper-bearing hill in north Anglesey. Bayesian modelling of radiocarbon dates places dated Early Bronze Age mining probably from 2085 to 1485 BC. A Roman attribution is known from gazetteer tradition and stamped Anglesey ingots, but no dated Roman underground workings have been identified.
new_values.$[5].uncertainty: The Early Bronze Age dates are modelled ranges (95%: 2245–1300 BC; 68% start/end: 2085–1890 and 1735–1485), not observed years. No dated Roman workings survive; the Roman mining attribution is circumstantial and must not be shown as definite. Later opencast mining destroyed much of the evidence.

app_claim: Llyn Cerrig Bach: offerings were placed in the lake from -300 to 100; more than 150 iron and bronze objects were found in 1942-3. The entity has an empty sources array.
problem: The dated claim and object interpretation have no resolvable citation in the app, even though an Amgueddfa Cymru article directly supports the 300 BC–AD 100 deposition range and identifies chariots, weapons, tools and decorated metalwork found in the lake.

evidence.title: Ancient Druids of Wales
evidence.what_it_says: “Here, between 300BC and AD100, chariots, weapons, tools and decorated metalwork items were cast from a causeway or island into a small lake.” It says a large quantity of Iron Age metalwork was found in this lake during 1943.

app_claim: Caerleon phase 1: “Reduced occupation of the fortress” from 300 to 400, size 2, on a high-confidence entity.
problem: The visible phase implies another half-century of reduced fortress occupation, but the cited Pleiades record ends the legion’s base at ca. AD 300. The Roman Legion Museum’s later chronology says some buildings were used into the mid-4th century and streets were resurfaced after AD 346/348, but little happened after about 350. Extending the occupation phase to AD 400 overstates the current evidence.

evidence.title: Isca Silurum (Pleiades place 79532)
evidence.what_it_says: “Base of Legio II Augusta from ca. A.D. 75-300.”

evidence.title: Chronology
evidence.what_it_says: Some buildings were in use into the mid-4th century; streets were resurfaced after AD 346/348; little happened after about AD 350.

$[8].phases[1].label: Reduced occupation; streets resurfaced after about AD 346/8

new_values.$[8].uncertainty: Pleiades gives c. AD 75-300 for the legion’s base. The Roman Legion Museum notes some mid-4th-century building use and street resurfacing after AD 346/348, but little after about 350. What happened between the mid-4th century and the Norman castle recorded in Domesday Book is poorly known; 1086 is that record date.

wal-rlm-caerleon-chronology.title: Caerleon Roman Fortress and Baths: Chronology

app_claim: Deceangli: a people of north-east Wales, -100 to 200, attacked by Ostorius Scapula about AD 48; lead ingots from Flintshire of the AD 70s are stamped with their name. The sources array is empty and the note says no source was fetched.
problem: This checkable Roman-period claim has no resolvable citation. RIB 2404.32 directly records the AD 74 lead mark and discusses the Deceangli/Deceangi name, but RIB also warns that the precise ancient name is uncertain.

evidence.title: RIB 2404.32
evidence.what_it_says: The lead mark is dated to AD 74 and reads DECEANGL. Its commentary says the lead came from mines in the territory of the Flintshire tribe, but says it is uncertain whether that tribe was called Ceangi, Deceangi, Decangi (Tacitus) or Deceangli.

wal-rib-2404-32.title: RIB 2404.32: Vespasianic lead pig from the Deceangli

new_values.$[3].note: The people of north-east Wales, attacked by the Roman governor Ostorius Scapula about AD 48. A lead ingot from Flintshire dated AD 74 is marked DECEANGL; RIB notes uncertainty over whether the tribe’s name was Ceangi, Deceangi, Decangi or Deceangli. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD; projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary. The end date is a placeholder.

app_claim: Llandaff: “Early church community” from 600 to 1120, then “Cathedral”; Bishop Urban began the present cathedral in 1120 and the Book of Llandaff was compiled to back its claims. The sources array is empty.
problem: The entity’s date, saint associations and building claim are checkable and have no resolvable citation. The Cathedral’s own history directly supports a Christian presence from at least the 6th century and the present building from around 1120 under Bishop Urban.

evidence.title: History of the Cathedral
evidence.what_it_says: There has been a Christian presence on the site from at least the 6th century under Dyfrig and Teilo; the present building dates from the Norman period, around 1120, when Bishop Urban brought St Dyfrig’s remains to Llandaff.

evidence.title: The Book of Llandaff
evidence.what_it_says: The Book of Llandaff was written between 1120 and 1140 under Bishop Urban to strengthen the rights of the diocese. It includes the lives of Dyfrig, Teilo and Euddogwy and charters, some authentic and some later forgeries.

new_values.$[22].uncertainty: The early history rests on 12th-century documents written to support the bishopric; the start date is a placeholder. The cathedral’s own history records Christian presence from at least the 6th century and the present building from around 1120. The National Library of Wales notes that some Book of Llandaff charters are later forgeries.

app_claim: Dinas Powys hillfort phase 0: “Post-Roman chieftain’s stronghold” from 450 to 700, size 1. Summary: “Imported Mediterranean and Gaulish pottery, glass and fine metalworking show a wealthy household of the 5th to 7th centuries.”
problem: The app uses a broad traditional span and has no source. The 2023 Antiquity chronology models the dated activity as beginning cal AD 510–600 (95%) and ending cal AD 590–680 (95%), with abandonment in the later seventh or eighth century. It starts the site fifty years earlier than even the broad 95% model and continues it to 700 without recording the modelled end range.

evidence.title: A new chronology for the Welsh hillfort of Dinas Powys
evidence.what_it_says: The article says Alcock’s 1953–58 excavation recovered the largest fifth- to seventh-century post-Roman assemblage in Wales. Bayesian modelling of new radiocarbon dates suggests dated activity began cal AD 510–600 (95% probability) and ended cal AD 590–680 (95% probability); its revised phasing places abandonment in the later seventh or eighth century.

$[29].phases[0].label: Post-Roman chieftain’s stronghold
$[29].phases[0].note: Bayesian model: activity began cal AD 510–600 (95%) and ended cal AD 590–680 (95%); the representative 510–680 span should not be read as observed years.

new_values.$[29].summary: A small defended hilltop near Cardiff, excavated by Leslie Alcock in the 1950s and re-analysed in 2023. Imported Mediterranean and Gaulish pottery, glass and fine metalworking show a wealthy household. Bayesian modelling places the dated activity mainly in the sixth to seventh centuries, with abandonment in the later seventh or eighth century.
new_values.$[29].uncertainty: The rampart chronology has been revised repeatedly. The 2023 model gives activity beginning cal AD 510–600 (95%) and ending cal AD 590–680 (95%), but these are probability ranges, not observed years. Some material is earlier or residual, and the exact abandonment date is not fixed.

wal-antiquity-dinas-powys-chronology.title: A new chronology for the Welsh hillfort of Dinas Powys

app_claim: Conwy phase 0: “Aberconwy Abbey” from 1186 to 1283 at the Conwy marker. Its uncertainty says the abbey was “founded 1186, on this site from the 1190s.”
problem: The phase places the abbey at Conwy from its foundation year, but Aberconwy was founded in 1186 at Rhedynog Felen south of Caernarfon and only moved to the mouth of the Conwy by 1192. The current Conwy feature is therefore shown six years before it existed there.

evidence.title: Aberconwy 1 — Foundation, 1186
evidence.what_it_says: Aberconwy was founded on 24 July 1186, but the original site was at Rhedynog-felen, Conwy, south of Caernarfon; by 1192 the monks had resettled near the mouth of the River Conwy.

evidence.title: Aberconwy 1 — Relocation, 1192
evidence.what_it_says: The monks relocated from Rhedynog-fel because of its austere conditions; by 1192 the community had settled at a new site near the mouth of the River Conwy and remained there until the late thirteenth century.

new_values.$[41].phases[0].label: Aberconwy Abbey at the mouth of the Conwy
new_values.$[41].summary: Edward I and Master James of St George built the castle and a 1.3 km circuit of town walls here between 1283 and 1287. The site had held the Cistercian abbey of Aberconwy from 1192, burial place of Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, after its move from Rhedynog Felen; the king moved the community up the valley to Maenan in 1283.
new_values.$[41].uncertainty: Aberconwy was founded in 1186 at Rhedynog Felen south of Caernarfon and moved to the mouth of the Conwy by 1192, so this marker begins only with the Conwy-site phase. The later move to Maenan and the castle-building dates are well documented.

app_claim: Strata Florida phase 0: “Cistercian abbey” from 1164 to 1539 at the present abbey marker. Its uncertainty says the first community may have been on a different site before moving here in the 1180s.
problem: The phase places the abbey at the present Teifi site from 1164, but Cadw says Strata Florida has stood there since 1184. The earlier 1164 foundation belongs to the community’s first site, not the feature shown at this coordinate.

evidence.title: Strata Florida Abbey
evidence.what_it_says: Strata Florida “has stood on lush meadows beside the banks of the river Teifi since 1184.”

new_values.$[53].phases[0].label: Strata Florida Abbey at its Teifi site
new_values.$[53].summary: A Cistercian abbey in the Ceredigion uplands. The community was founded in 1164 on an earlier site and moved to the present Teifi site in 1184 under the patronage of the Lord Rhys. The monks entered their new church in 1201. Welsh princes were buried here and it supported the Welsh cause; it closed by 1539.
new_values.$[53].uncertainty: The first community was founded in 1164 but may have begun on a different site nearby; Cadw dates the present site to 1184. This marker therefore starts only with the abbey’s Teifi-site phase. The closure date is 1539.

app_claim: Basingwerk phase 0: “Abbey (Savigniac, then Cistercian)” from 1131 to 1536 at the present abbey marker. Its uncertainty says the first community may have been at a different site nearby.
problem: The phase places the abbey at the present ruins from its c.1131 foundation, but Monastic Wales says the first site may have been Coleshill, about 5 km south-east, and records a likely site relocation in 1157 when Basingwerk became a dependency of Buildwas. The current feature is therefore shown up to about 26 years before it can be placed on that site.

evidence.title: Basingwerk — Foundation, c. 1131
evidence.what_it_says: The community likely arrived in 1131, but the first site may have been Coleshill, around 5 km south-east of the current ruins, or closer to the present site; discussion continues.

evidence.title: Site details: Basingwerk
evidence.what_it_says: The site history records the 1157 event “Basingwerk became a dependency of Buildwas and likely moved site at this time.”

new_values.$[57].phases[0].label: Basingwerk Abbey on its present site (Savigniac, then Cistercian)
new_values.$[57].summary: An abbey near Holywell on the Dee estuary, founded as a Savigniac house in c.1131 and probably moved to the present site in 1157 when it became a dependency of Buildwas; it entered the Cistercian Order in 1147 and was much rebuilt in the 13th century. Wat’s Dyke reaches the estuary close by.
new_values.$[57].uncertainty: The community was founded c.1131, but Monastic Wales says its first site may have been Coleshill or another nearby location and that it likely moved to the present site in 1157. The marker therefore begins only with the present-site phase. Cadw dates dissolution to 1536, while Monastic Wales gives late 1536 to spring 1537.
